football: An inflated ball to be kicked in sport, usually made in India rubber, or a bladder incased in Leather. Waller. 2. The game of kicking the football by opposing parties of players between goals. Arbuthnot.
forestay: A large, strong rope, reaching from the foremast head to the bowsprit, to support the mast. See Illust. under Ship.
fog: (a) A second growth of grass; aftergrass. (b) Dead or decaying grass remaining on land through the winter; -- called also foggage. [Prov.Eng.] Halliwell. Note: Sometimes called, in New England, old… | (Agric.) To pasture cattle on the fog, or aftergrass, of; to eat off the fog from.
foe: See Fiend, and cf. Feud a quarrel. 1. One who entertains personal enmity, hatred, grudge, or malice, against another; an enemy. A man's foes shall be they of his own household. Matt. x. 36 2. | To treat as an enemy. (old) Spenser.
foreclose: To shut up or out; to preclude; to stop; to prevent; to bar; to exclude. The embargo with Spain foreclosed this trade. Carew. To foreclose a mortgager (Law), to cut him off by a judgment of court from the power of redeeming the mortgaged premises, termed his equity of redemption.
fondon: A large copper vessel used for hot amalgamation.
fop: One whose ambition it is to gain admiration by showy dress; a coxcomb; an inferior dandy.
fountain: 1. A spring of water issuing from the earth. 2. An artificially produced jet or stream of water; also, the structure or works in which such a jet or stream rises or flows; a basin built and constantly supplied with pure water for drinking and other useful purposes, or for ornament. 3.
footmark: A footprint; a track or vestige. Coleridge.
fosterage: The care of a foster child; the charge of nursing. Sir W. Raleigh.
fortifier: One who, or that which, fortifies, strengthens, supports, or upholds.
foreignism: Anything peculiar to a foreign language or people; a foreign idiom or custom. It is a pity to see the technicalities of the so-called liberal professions distigured by foreignisms. Fitzed. Hall.
fondus: A style of printing calico, paper hangings, etc., in which the colors are in bands and graduated into each other. Ure.
footbreadth: The breadth of a foot; -- used as a measure. Longfellow. Not so much as a footbreadth. Deut. ii. 5.
footguards: Infantry soldiers belonging to select regiments called the Guards. [Eng.]
forby: Near; hard by; along; past. (old) To tell her if her child went ought forby. Chaucer. To the intent that ships may pass along forby all the sides of the city without let. Robynson (More's Utopia).
fourpence: 1. A British silver coin, worth four pence; a groat. 2. A name formerly given in New England to the Spanish half real, a silver coin worth six and a quarter cents.
focalize: To bring to a focus; to focus; to concentrate. Light is focalized in the eye, sound in the ear. De Quincey.
footstep: 1. The mark or impression of the foot; a track; hence, visible sign of a course pursued; token; mark; as, the footsteps of divine wisdom. How on the faltering footsteps of decay Youth presses. Bryant. 2. An inclined plane under a hand printing press.
foots: The settlings of oil, molasses, etc., at the bottom of a barrel or hogshead. Simmonds.
forget: 1. To lose the remembrance of; to let go from the memory; to cease to have in mind; not to think of; also, to lose the power of; to cease from doing. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits. Ps. ciii. 2. Let y right hand forget her cunning. Ps. cxxxvii. 5. Hath thy knee forget to bow Shak. 2. To treat with inattention or disregard; to slight; to neglect.
foretell: To predict; to tell before occurence; to prophesy; to foreshow. Deeds then undone my faithful tongue foretold. Pope. Prodigies, foretelling the future eminence and luster of his character. C. | To utter predictions. Acts iii. 24.
foxery: Behavior like that of a fox; (old) Chaucer.
forswearer: One who rejects of renounces upon oath; one who swears a false oath.
foinery: Thrusting with the foil; fencing with the point, as distinguished from broadsword play. (old) Marston.
fondling: The act of caressing; manifestation of tenderness. Cyrus made no . . . amorous fondling To fan her pride, or melt her guardless heart. Mickle. | 1. A person or thing fondled or caressed; one treated with foolish or doting affection. Fondlings are in danger to be made fools. L'Estrange. 2. A fool; a simpleton; a ninny. (old) Chapman.
foreread: To tell beforehand; to signify by tokens; to predestine. (old) Spenser.
formula: 1. A prescribed or set form; an established rule; a fixed or conventional method in which anything is to be done, arranged, or said. 2. (Eccl.) A written confession of faith; a formal statement of foctrines. 3. (Math.) A rule or principle expressed in algebraic language; as, the binominal formula. 4. (Med.) A prescription or recipe for the preparation of a medicinal compound.
fornicator: An unmarried person, male or female, who has criminal intercourse with the other sex; one guilty of fornication.
formaldehyde: A colorless, volatile liquid, H2CO, resembling acetic or ethyl aldehyde, and chemically intermediate between methyl alcohol and formic acid.
foy: 1. Faith; allegiance; fealty. (old) Spenser. 2. A feast given by one about to leave a place. (old) He did at the Dog give me, and some other friends of his, his foy, he being to set sail to-day. Pepys.
foumart: The European polecat; -- called also European ferret, and fitchew. See Polecat. [Written also foulmart, foulimart, and fulimart.]
foolfish: (a) The orange filefish. See Filefish. (b) The winter flounder. See Flounder.
foursome: Consisting of four; requiring four participants. [Scot. or Golf] | A game between four players, with two on each side and each side playing but one ball, the partners striking alternately. It is called a mixed foursome when each side consists of a man and a woman.
folding: 1. The act of making a fold or folds; also, a fold; a doubling; a plication. The lower foldings of the vest. Addison. 2. (Agric.) The keepig of sheep in inclosures on arable land, etc. Folding boat, a portable boat made by stretching canvas, etc., over jointed framework, used in campaigning, and by tourists, etc. Ham. Nav. Encyc.
foresee: 1. To see beforehand; to have prescience of; to foreknow. A prudent man foreseeth the evil. Prov. xxii. 3. 2. To provide. (old) Great shoals of people, which go on to populate, without foreseeing… | To have or exercise foresight. (old)
forwarding: 1. The act of one who forwards; the act or occupation of transmitting merchandise or other property for others. 2. (Bookbinding) The process of putting a book into its cover, and making it ready for the finisher.
fortyspot: The Tasmanian forty-spotted diamond bird (Pardalotus quadragintus).
footstool: A low stool to support the feet of one when sitting.
forestal: Of or pertaining to forests; as, forestal rights.
footfall: A setting down of the foot; a footstep; the sound of a footstep. Shak. Seraphim, whose footfalls tinkled on the tufted floor. Poe
formulary: 1. A book containing stated and prescribed forms, as of oaths, declarations, prayers, medical formulaæ, etc.; a book of precedents. 2. Prescribed form or model; formula.
fourscore: The product of four times twenty; eighty units or objects.
forewarn: To warn beforehand; to give previous warning, admonition, information, or notice to; to caution in advance. We were forewarned of your coming. Shak.
foreshorten: 1. (Fine Art) To represent on a plane surface, as if extended in a direction toward the spectator or nearly so; to shorten by drawing in perspective. 2. Fig.: To represent pictorially to the imagination. Songs, and deeds, and lives that lie Foreshortened in the tract of time. Tennyson.
foreship: The fore part of a ship. (old)
foussa: A viverrine animal of Madagascar (Cryptoprocta ferox). It resembles a cat in size and form, and has retractile claws.
forger: One who forges, makes, of forms; a fabricator; a falsifier. 2. Especially: One guilty of forgery; one who makes or issues a counterfeit document.
foxlike: Resembling a fox in his characteristic qualities; cunning; artful; foxy.
forgetful: 1. Apt to forget; easily losing remembrance; as, a forgetful man should use helps to strengthen his memory. 2. Heedless; careless; neglectful; inattentive. Be not forgetful to entertain strangers. Heb. xiii. 2. 3. Causing to forget; inducing oblivion; oblivious. [Archaic or Poetic] "The forgetful wine." J. Webster.
foreshow: To show or exhibit beforehand; to give foreknowledge of; to prognosticate; to foretell. Your looks foreshow You have a gentle heart. Shak. Next, like Aurora, Spenser rose, Whose purple blush the day foreshows. Denham.
footrope: (a) The rope rigged below a yard, upon which men stand when reefing or furling; -- formerly called a horse. (b) That part of the boltrope to which the lower edge of a sail is sewed.
fossane: A species of civet (Viverra fossa) resembling the genet.
foundry: 1. The act, process, or art of casting metals. 2. The buildings and works for casting metals. Foundry ladle, a vessel for holding molten metal and conveying it from cupola to the molds.
forspent: Wasted in strength; tired; exhausted. (old) A gentleman almost forspent with speed. Shak.
forayer: One who makes or joins in a foray. They might not choose the lowand road, For the Merse forayers were abroad. Sir W. Scott.
fougade: A small mine, in the form of a well sunk from the surface of the ground, charged with explosive and projectiles. It is made in a position likely to be occupied by the enemy.
formidableness: The quality of being formidable, or adapted to excite dread. Boyle.
forcipal: Forked or branched like a pair of forceps; constructed so as to open and shut like a pair of forceps. Sir T. Browne.
foreleader: One who leads others by his example; aguide.
foreadvise: To advise or counsel before the time of action, or before the event. Shak.
fossorious: Adapted for digging; -- said of the legs of certain insects.
foolhardy: Daring without judgment; foolishly adventurous and bold. Howell. Syn. -- Rash; venturesome; venturous; precipitate; reckless; headlong; incautious. See Rash.
found: To form by melting a metal, and pouring it into a mold; to cast. "Whereof to found their engines." Milton. | A thin, single-cut file for combmakers.
formic: Pertaining to, or derived from, ants; as, formic acid; in an extended sense, pertaining to, or derived from, formic acid; as, formic ether. Amido formic acid, carbamic acid.
forthright: Straight forward; in a straight direction. (old) Sir P. Sidney. | Direct; straightforward; as, a forthright man. (old) Lowell. They were Night and Day, and Day and Night, Piligrims wight with steps forthright. Emerson.
foulness: The quality or condition of being foul.
foreground: On a painting, and sometimes in a bas-relief, mosaic picture, or the like, that part of the scene represented, which is nearest to the spectator, and therefore occupies the lowest part of the work of art itself. Cf. Distance, n., 6.
footfight: A conflict by persons on foot; -- distinguished from a fight on horseback. Sir P. Sidney.
forktail: (a) One of several Asiatic and East Indian passerine birds, belonging to Enucurus, and allied genera. The tail is deeply forking. (b) A salmon in its fourth year's growth. [Prov. Eng.]
fond: 1. Foolish; silly; simple; weak. (old) Grant I may never prove so fond To trust man on his oath or bond. Shak. 2. Foolishly tender and loving; weakly indulgent; over-affectionate. 3. Affectionate; | To caress; to fondle. (old) The Tyrian hugs and fonds thee on her breast. Dryden.
formicaroid: Like or pertaining to the family Formicaridæ or ant thrushes.
foxearth: A hole in the earth to which a fox resorts to hide himself.
forceless: Having little or no force; feeble. These forceless flowers like sturdy trees support me. Shak.
foreskirt: The front skirt of a garment, in distinction from the train. Honor's train Is longer than his foreskirt. Shak.
forcepump: (a) A pump having a solid piston, or plunger, for drawing and forcing a liquid, as water, through the valves; in distinction from a pump having a bucket, or valved piston. (b) A pump adapted for delivering water at a considerable height above the pump, or under a considerable pressure;
format: The shape and size of a book; hence, its external form. The older manuscripts had been written in a much larger format than that found convenient for university work. G. H. Putnam. One might, indeed, protest that the format is a little too luxurious. Nature.
formidable: Exciting fear or apprehension; impressing dread; adapted to excite fear and deter from approach, encounter, or undertaking; alarming. They seemed to fear the formodable sight. Dryden. I swell my preface into a volume, and make it formidable, when you see so many pages behind. Drydn. Syn. -- Dreadful; fearful; terrible; frightful; shocking; horrible; terrific; tremendous.
foggy: 1. Filled or abounding with fog, or watery exhalations; misty; as, a foggy atmosphere; a foggy morning. Shak. 2. Beclouded; dull; obscure; as, foggy ideas. Your coarse, foggy, drowsy conceit. Hayward.
foolify: To make a fool of; to befool. Holland.
fourteenth: 1. Next in order after the thirteenth; as, the fourteenth day of the month. 2. Making or constituting one of fourteen equal parts into which anything may be derived. | 1. One of fourteen equal parts into which one whole may be divided; the quotient of a unit divided by fourteen; one next after the thirteenth. 2. (Mus.) The octave of the seventh.
foxy: 1. Like or pertaining to the fox; foxlike in disposition or looks; wily. Modred's narrow, foxy face. Tennyson. 2. Having the color of a fox; of a yellowish or reddish brown color; -- applied sometimes to paintings when they have too much of this color. 3. Having the odor of a fox; rank; strong smeelling. 4. Sour; unpleasant in taste;
forslugge: To lsoe by idleness or slotch. (old) Chaucer.
foam: The white substance, consisting of an aggregation of bubbles, which is formed on the surface of liquids,or in the mouth of an animal, by violent agitation or fermentation; froth; spume; scum; | 1. formicate: Resembling, or pertaining to, an ant or ants.
footsore: Having sore or tender feet, as by reason of much walking; as, foot-sore cattle.
forgetter: One who forgets; a heedless person. Johnson.
fourchette: 1. A table fork. 2. (Anat.) (a) A small fold of membrane, connecting the labia in the posterior part of the vulva. (b) The wishbone or furculum of birds. (c) The frog of the hoof of the horse and allied animals. 3. (Surg.) An instrument used to raise and support the tongue during the cutting of the frænum. 4.
forwards: Toward a part or place before or in front; onward; in advance; progressively; -- opposed to backward.
forehearth: The forward extension of the hearth of a blast furnace under the tymp.
forold: Very old. (old) A bear's skin, coal-black, forold. Chaucer.
foliar: Consisting of, or pertaining to, leaves; as, foliar appendages. Foliar gap (Bot.), an opening in the fibrovascular system of a stem at the point of origin of a leaf. -- Foliar trace (Bot.), a particular fibrovascular bundle passing down into the stem from a leaf.
foraminifera: An extensive order of rhizopods which generally have a chambered calcareous shell formed by several united zooids. Many of them have perforated walls, whence the name. Some species are covered with sand. See Rhizophoda.
foretaster: One who tastes beforehand, or before another.
forlay: To lie in wait for; to ambush. An ambushed thief forlays a traveler. Dryden.
footton: A unit of energy or work, being equal to the work done in raising one ton against the force of gravity through the height of one foot.
foolhappy: Lucky, without judgment or contrivance. (old) Spenser.
fool: A compound of gooseberries scalded and crushed, with cream; -- commonly called gooseberry fool. | 1. One destitute of reason, or of the common powers of understanding; an idiot; a natural. 2. forslack: To neglect by idleness; to delay or to waste by sloth. (old) Spenser.
forte: 1. The strong point; that in which one excels. fort"a The construction of a fable seems by no means the forte of our modern poetical writers. Jeffrey. 2. The stronger part of the blade of a sword; the part of half nearest the hilt; -- opposed to foible.
fogbelt: A region of the ocean where fogs are of marked frequency, as near the coast of Newfoundland.
folk: 1. (Eng. Hist.) In Anglo-Saxon times, the people of a group of townships or villages; a community; a tribe. (old) The organization of each folk, as such, sprang mainly from war. J. R. Green. 2. People in general, or a separate class of people; -- generally used in the plural form, and often with a qualifying adjective; as, the old folks; poor folks.
foretooth: One of the teeth in the forepart of the mouth; an incisor.
formedon: A writ of right for a tenant in tail in case of a discontinuance of the estate tail. This writ has been abolished.
fougasse: A small mine, in the form of a well sunk from the surface of the ground, charged with explosive and projectiles. It is made in a position likely to be occupied by the enemy.
fovilla: One of the fine granules contained in the protoplasm of a pollen grain.
foothot: Hastily; immediately; instantly; on the spot; hotfloot. Gower. Custance have they taken anon, foothot. Chaucer.
foreordination: Previous ordination or appointment; predetermination; predestination.
fomalhaut: A star of the first magnitude, in the constellation Piscis Australis, or Southern Fish.
foolhardihood: The state of being foolhardy; foolhardiness.
fossa: A pit, groove, cavity, or depression, of greater or less depth; as, the temporal fossa on the side of the skull; the nasal fossæ containing the nostrils in most birds.
fortissimo: Very loud; with the utmost strength or loudness.
forcipation: Torture by pinching with forceps or pinchers. Bacon.
forespeak: To foretell; to predict. (old) My mother was half a witch; never anything that she forespake but came to pass. Beau. & Fl.
founder: One who founds, establishes, and erects; one who lays a foundation; an author; one from whom anything originates; one who endows. | One who founds; one who casts metals in various forms; a caster; as, a founder of cannon, bells, hardware, or types. Fonder's dust. Same as Facing, 4. -- Founder's sand, a kind of sand suitable for…
forespent: Already spent; gone by; past. (old) Shak.
formule: A set or prescribed model; a formula. (old) Johnson.
forsythia: A shrub of the Olive family, with yellow blossoms.
forenenst: Over against; opposite to. [Now dialectic] The land forenenst the Greekish shore. Fairfax.
foremilk: The milk secreted just before, or directly after, the birth of a child or of the young of an animal; colostrum.
forethought: Thought of, or planned, beforehand; aforethought; prepense; hence, deliberate. "Forethought malice." Bacon. | A thinking or planning beforehand; prescience; premeditation; forecast; provident care. A sphere that will demand from him forethought, courage, and wisdom. I. Taylor.
foregame: A first game; first plan. (old) Whitlock.
forecastle: (a) A short upper deck forward, formerly raised like a castle, to command an enemy's decks. (b) That part of the upper deck of a vessel forward of the foremast, or of the after part of the fore channels. (c) In merchant vessels, the forward part of the vessel, under the deck, where the sailors live.
foully: In a foul manner; filthily; nastily; shamefully; unfairly; dishonorably. I foully wronged him; do forgive me, do. Gay.
forfeitable: Liable to be forfeited; subject to forfeiture. For the future, uses shall be subject to the statutes of mortmain, and forfeitable, like the lands themselves. Blackstone.
fourling: 1. One of four children born at the same time. 2. (Crystallog.) A compound or twin crystal consisting of four individuals.
foretopmast: The mast erected at the head of the foremast, and at the head of which stands the fore-topgallant mast. See Ship.
foregleam: An antecedent or premonitory gleam; a dawning light. The foregleams of wisdom. Whittier.
fowl: 1. Any bird; esp., any large edible bird. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air. Gen. i. 26. Behold the fowls of the air; for they sow not. Matt. vi. 26. | To catch or kill wild fowl, for game or food, as by shooting, or by decoys, nets, etc. Such persons as may lawfully hunt, fish, or fowl. Blackstone. Fowling piece, a light gun with smooth bore,…
foreslow: To make slow; to hinder; to obstruct. (old) See Forslow, v. t. No stream, no wood, no mountain could foreslow Their hasty pace. Fairfax. | To loiter. (old) See Forslow, v. i.
footpath: A narrow path or way for pedestrains only; a footway.
fovea: A slight depression or pit; a fossa.
forfete: To incur a penalty; to transgress. (old) And all this suffered our Lord Jesus Christ that never forfeted. Chaucer.
fonde: To endeavor; to strive; to try. (old) Chaucer.
forereach: To advance or gain upon; -- said of a vessel that gains upon another when sailing closehauled. | To shoot ahead, especially when going in stays. R. H. Dana, Jr.
forcible: 1. Possessing force; characterized by force, efficiency, or energy; powerful; efficacious; impressive; influential. How forcible are right words! Job. vi. 2 Sweet smells are most forcible in dry substances, when broken. Bacon. But I have reasons strong and forcible. Shak. That punishment which hath been sometimes forcible to bridle sin. Hooker.
fortition: Casual choice; fortuitous selection; hazard. No mode of election operating in the spirit of fortition or rotation can be generally good. Burke.
fossores: A group of hymenopterous insects including the sand wasps. They excavate cells in earth, where they deposit their eggs, with the bodies of other insects for the food of the young when hatched. [Written also Fossoria.]
fomenter: One who foments; one who encourages or instigates; as, a fomenter of sedition.
forcing: 1. The accomplishing of any purpose violently, precipitately, prematurely, or with unusual expedition. 2. (Gardening) The art of raising plants, flowers, and fruits at an earlier season than the natural one, as in a hitbed or by the use of artificial heat.
formulize: To reduce to a formula; to formulate. Emerson.
foresail: (a) The sail bent to the foreyard of a square-rigged vessel, being the lowest sail on the foremast. (b) The gaff sail set on the foremast of a schooner. (c) The fore staysail of a sloop, being the triangular sail next forward of the mast.
forehew: To hew or cut in front. (old) Sackville.
forhall: To harass; to torment; to distress. (old) Spenser.
form: A suffix used to denote in the form or shape of, resembling, etc.; as, valiform; oviform. | 1. The shape and structure of anything, as distinguished from the material of which it is composed; particular disposition or arrangement of matter, giving it individuality or distinctive character;
forgiveness: 1. The act of forgiving; the state of being forgiven; as, the forgiveness of sin or of injuries. To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses. Dan. ix. 9. In whom we have . . . the forgiveness of sin. Eph. i. 7. 2. Disposition to pardon; willingness to forgive.
foreknowable: That may be foreknown. Dr. H. More.
forefeel: To feel beforehand; to have a presentiment of. (old) As when, with unwieldy waves, the great sea forefeels winds. Chapman.
forky: Opening into two or more parts or shoots; forked; furcated. "Forky tongues." Pope.
foray: A sudden or irregular incursion in border warfare; hence, any irregular incursion for war or spoils; a raid. Spenser. The huge Earl Doorm, . . . Bound on a foray, rolling eyes of prey. Tennyson. | To pillage; to ravage. He might foray our lands. Sir W. Scott.
forbidding: Repelling approach; repulsive; raising abhorrence, aversion, or dislike; disagreeable; prohibiting or interdicting; as, a forbidding aspect; a forbidding formality; a forbidding air. formulization: The act or process of reducing to a formula; the state of being formulized.
fortunately: In a fortunate manner; luckily; successfully; happily.
foreright: Ready; directly forward; going before. (old) "A foreright wind." Chapman.
folkmoter: One who takes part in a folkmote, or local court. (old) Milton.
foxfish: (a) The fox shark; -- called also sea fox. See Thrasher shark, under Shark. (b) The european dragonet. See Dragonet.
fortieth: 1. Following the thirty-ninth, or preceded by thirty-nine units, things, or parts. 2. fore: Journey; way; method of proceeding. (old) "Follow him and his fore." Chaucer. | 1. In the part that precedes or goes first; -- opposed to aft, after, back, behind, etc. 2. Formerly; previously; afore. [Obs. or Colloq.] The eyes, fore duteous, now converted are. Shak. 3.
foreland: 1. A promontory or cape; a headland; as, the North and South Foreland in Kent, England. 2. (Fort.) A piece of ground between the wall of a place and the moat. Farrow. 3. (Hydraul. Engin.) That portion of the natural shore on the outside of the embankment which receives the stock of waves and deadens their force. Knight.
forejudge: To judge beforehand, or before hearing the facts and proof; to prejudge. | To expel from court for some offense or misconduct, as an attorney or officer; to deprive or put out of a thing by the judgment of a court. Burrill.
forbear: An ancestor; a forefather; -- usually in the plural. [Scot.] "Your forbears of old." Sir W. Scott. | 1. To refrain from proceeding; to pause; to delay. Shall I go against Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I forbear 1 Kinds xxii. 6. 2. To refuse; to decline; to give no heed.
foresight: 1. The act or the power of foreseeing; prescience; foreknowledge. Milton. 2. Action in reference to the future; provident care; prudence; wise forethought. font: A complete assortment of printing type of one size, including a due proportion of all the letters in the alphabet, large and small, points, accents, and whatever else is necessary for printing with… | 1. A fountain; a spring; a source. Bathing forever in the font of bliss. Young. 2. A basin or stone vessel in which water is contained for baptizing. That name was given me at the font. Shak.
foundationer: One who derives support from the funds or foundation of a college or school. [Eng.]
fourb: A trickly fellow; a cheat. (old) Evelyn. Denham.
foresay: To foretell. (old) Her danger nigh that sudden change foresaid. Fairfax.
foliation: 1. The process of forming into a leaf or leaves. 2. The manner in which the young leaves are dispo The . . . foliation must be in relation to the stem. De Quincey. 3. The act of beating a metal into a thin plate, leaf, foil, or lamina. 4. The act of coating with an amalgam of tin foil and quicksilver, as in making looking-glasses. 5.
footvalve: A suction valve or check valve at the lower end of a pipe; esp., such a valve in a steam-engine condenser opening to the air pump.
forepart: The part most advanced, or first in time or in place; the beginning.
fossil: 1. Dug out of the eart; as, fossil coal; fossil salt. 2. (Paleon.) Like or pertaining to fossils; contained in rocks. whether petrified or not; as, fossil plants, shells. | 1. A substance dug from the earth. (old) Note: Formerly all minerals were called fossils, but the word is now restricted to express the remains of animals and plants found buried in the earth. Ure.
fondly: 1. Foolishly. (old) Verstegan (1673). Make him speak fondly like a frantic man. Shak. 2. In a fond manner; affectionately; tenderly. My heart, untarveled, fondly turns to thee. Goldsmith.
forted: Furnished with, or guarded by, forts; strengthened or defended, as by forts. Shak.
foreworn: Worn out; wasted; used up. (old) Old foreworn stories almost forgotten. Brydges.
formally: In a formal manner; essentially; characteristically; expressly; regularly; ceremoniously; precisely. That which formally makes this [charity] a Christian grace, is the spring from which it flows. Smalridge. You and your followers do stand formally divided against the authorized guides of the church and rest of the people. Hooker.
forcer: 1. One who, or that which, forces or drives. 2. (Mech.) (a) The solid piston of a force pump; the instrument by which water is forced in a pump. (b) A small hand pump for sinking pits, draining cellars, etc.
foin: 1. (Zoöl.) The beech marten (Mustela foina). See Marten. 2. A kind of fur, black at the top on a whitish ground, taken from the ferret or weasel of the same name.(old) He came to the stake in a fair… | To thrust with a sword or spear; to lunge. (old) He stroke, he soused, he foynd, he hewed, he lashed. Spenser. They lash, they foin, they pass, they strive to bore Their corselets, and the thinnest…
fourcycle: A four-stroke cycle, as the Otto cycle, for an internal- combustion engine. -- Four"-cy`cle, a.
footlight: One of a row of lights in the front of the stage in a theater, etc., and on a level therewith. Before the footlights, upon the stage; -- hence, in the capacity of an actor.
foulard: A thin, washable material of silk, or silk and cotton, originally imported from India, but now also made elsewhere.
forgive: 1. To give wholly; to make over without reservation; to resign. To them that list the world's gay shows I leave, And to great ones such folly do forgive. Spenser. 2. To give up resentment or claim to requital on account of (an offense or wrong); to remit the penalty of; to pardon; -- said in reference to the act forgiven. And their sins should be forgiven them. Mark iv. 12.
forenight: The evening between twilight and bedtime. [Scot.]
foreclosure: The act or process of foreclosing; a proceeding which bars or extinguishes a mortgager's right of redeeming a mortgaged estate.
foremostly: In the foremost place or order; among the foremost. J. Webster.
fogbow: A nebulous arch, or bow, of white or yellowish light sometimes seen in fog, etc.
fondness: 1. The quality or state of being fond; foolishness. (old) Fondness it were for any, being free, To covet fetters, though they golden be. Spenser. 2. Doting affection; tender liking; strong appetite, propensity, or relish; as, he had a fondness for truffles. My heart had still some foolish fondness for thee. Addison. Syn.- Attachment; affection; love; kindness.
foreskin: The fold of skin which covers the glans of the penis; the prepuce.
foolish: 1. Marked with, or exhibiting, folly; void of understanding; weak in intellect; without judgment or discretion; silly; unwise. I am a very foolish fond old man. Shak. 2. Such as a fool would do; proceeding from weakness of mind or silliness; exhibiting a want of judgment or discretion; as, a foolish act. 3. Absurd; ridiculous; despicable; contemptible.
forceps: 1. A pair of pinchers, or tongs; an instrument for grasping, holding firmly, or exerting traction upon, bodies which it would be inconvenient or impracticable to seize with the fingers, especially one for delicate operations, as those of watchmakers, surgeons, accoucheurs, dentists, etc. 2. (Zoöl.) The caudal forceps-shaped appendage of earwigs and some other insects.
forejudger: A judgment by which one is deprived or put of a right or thing in question.
forthrightness: Straightforwardness; explicitness; directness. (old) Dante's concise forthrightness of phrase. Hawthorne.
forlet: To give up; to leave; to abandon. (old) "To forlet sin." Chaucer.
fortnightly: Occurring or appearing once in a fortnight; as, a fortnightly meeting of a club; a fortnightly magazine, or other publication. -- adv. Once in a fortnight; at intervals of a fortnight.
fossilism: 1. The science or state of fossils. Coleridge. 2. The state of being extremely antiquated in views and opinions.
forefoot: 1. One of the anterior feet of a quardruped or multiped; -- usually written fore foot. 2. (Shipbuilding) A piece of timber which terminates the keel at the fore end, connecting it with the lower end of the stem.
folio: 1. A leaf of a book or manuscript. 2. A sheet of paper once folded. 3. A book made of sheets of paper each folded once (four pages to the sheet); hence, a book of the largest kind. | To put a serial number on each folio or page of (a book); to page.
foul: 1. Covered with, or containing, extraneous matter which is injurious, noxious, offensive, or obstructive; filthy; dirty; not clean; polluted; nasty; defiled; as, a foul cloth; foul hands; | 1. To make filthy; to defile; to daub; to dirty; to soil; as, to foul the face or hands with mire. 2. (Mil.) To incrust (the bore of a gun) with burnt powder in the process of firing. 3.
foodful: Full of food; supplying food; fruitful; fertile. "The foodful earth." Dryden. Bent by its foodful burden [the corn]. Glover.
fourbe: A trickly fellow; a cheat. (old) Evelyn. Denham.
forgetmenot: A small herb, of the genus Myosotis (M. palustris, incespitosa, etc.), bearing a beautiful blue flower, and extensively considered the emblem of fidelity. Note: Formerly the name was given to the Ajuga Chamæpitus.
fourhanded: 1. Having four hands; quadrumanous. Goldsmith. 2. Requiring four "hands" or players; as, a fourhanded game at cards.
forerecited: Named or recited before. "The forerecited practices." Shak.
formularize: To reduce to a forula; to formulate.
foretop: 1. The hair on the forepart of the head; esp., a tuft or lock of hair which hangs over the forehead, as of a horse. 2. That part of a headdress that is in front; the top of a periwig. 3. (Naut.) The platform at the head of the foremast.
fourway: Allowing passage in either of four directions; as, a four-way cock, or valve. Francis. Four-way cock, a cock connected with four pipes or ports, and having two or more passages in the plug, by which the adjacent pipes or ports may be made to communicate; formerly used as a valve in the steam engine, and now for various other purposes.
foretopgallant: Designating the mast, sail, yard, etc., above the topmast; as, the fore-topgallant sail. See Sail.
forelie: To lie in front of. (old) Which forelay Athwart her snowy breast. Spenser.
foreallege: To allege or cite before. Fotherby.
footed: 1. Having a foot or feet; shaped in the foot. "Footed like a goat." Grew. Note: Footed is often used in composition in the sense of having (such or so many) feet; as, fourfooted beasts. 2. Having a foothold; established. Our king . . . is footed in this land already. Shak.
forebodement: The act of foreboding; the thing foreboded.
forequoted: Cited before; quoted in a foregoing part of the treatise or essay.
forewoman: A woman who is chief; a woman who has charge of the work or workers in a shop or other place; a head woman. Tatler. W. Besant.
forbidden: Prohibited; interdicted. I kniw no spells, use no forbidden arts. Milton. Forbidden fruit. (a) Any coveted unlawful pleasure, -- so called with reference to the forbidden fruit of the Garden of Eden. (b) (Bot.) A small variety of shaddock (Citrus decumana). The name is given in different places to several varieties of Citrus fruits.
foreprize: To prize or rate beforehand. (old) Hooker.
fogginess: The state of being foggy. Johnson.
foliaged: Furnished with foliage; leaved; as, the variously foliaged mulberry.
foresighted: Sagacious; prudent; provident for the future. Bartram.
folklore: . Tales, legends, or superstitions long current among the people. Trench.
fossilization: The process of converting, or of being converted, into a fossil.
forelend: See Forlend. (old) As if that life to losse they had forelent. Spenser.
foehn: (a) A warm dry wind that often blows in the northern valleys of the Alps, due to the indraught of a storm center passing over Central Europe. The wind, heated by compression in its descent from the mountains, reaches the base, particularly in winter, dry and warm. (b) Any similar wind, as the chinook, in other parts of the world.
forenotice: Notice or information of an event before it happens; forewarning. Rymer.
footcandle: The amount of illumination produced by a standard candle at a distance of one foot.
foxed: 1. Discolored or stained; -- said of timber, and also of the paper of books or engravings. 2. Repaired by foxing; as, foxed boots.
forage: 1. The act of foraging; search for provisions, etc. He [the lion] from forage will incline to play. Shak. One way a band select from forage drives A herd of beeves, fair oxen and fair kine. Milton. | To wander or rove in search of food; to collect food, esp. forage, for horses and cattle by feeding on or stripping the country; to ravage; to feed on spoil. His most mighty father on a hill Stood…
fossilize: 1. To convert into a fossil; to petrify; as, to fossilize bones or wood. 2. To cause to become antiquated, rigid, or fixed, as by fossilization; to mummify; to deaden. | 1. To become fossil. 2. To become antiquated, rigid, or fixed, beyond the influence of change or progress.
formulation: The act, process, or result of formulating or reducing to a formula.
foreconceive: To preconceive; to imagine beforehand. (old) Bacon.
foot: 1. (Anat.) The terminal part of the leg of man or an animal; esp., the part below the ankle or wrist; that part of an animal upon which it rests when standing, or moves. See Manus, and Pes. 2. | 1. To tread to measure or music; to dance; to trip; to skip. Dryden. 2. To walk; -- opposed to ride or fly. Shak.
forgather: To convene; to gossip; to meet accidentally. [Scot.] Jamieson. Within that circle he forgathered with many a fool. Wilson.
forebode: 1. To foretell. 2. To be prescient of (some ill or misfortune); to have an inward conviction of, as of a calamity which is about to happen; to augur despondingly. His heart forebodes a mystery. | To fortell; to presage; to augur. If I forebode aright. Hawthorne.
forbiddance: The act of forbidding; prohibition; command or edict against a thing. (old) ow hast thou yield to transgress The strict forbiddance. Milton.
formularistic: Pertaining to, or exhibiting, formularization. Emerson.
foothill: A low hill at the foot of highe
forfeiter: One who incurs a penalty of forfeiture.
fort: A strong or fortified place; usually, a small fortified place, occupied only by troops, surrounded with a ditch, rampart, and parapet, or with palisades, stockades, or other means of defense; a fortification. Detached works, depending solely on their own strength, belong to the class of works termed forts. Farrow.
foreby: Near; hard by; along; past. See Forby. Spenser.
footpound: A unit of energy, or work, being equal to the work done in raising one pound avoirdupois against the force of gravity the height of one foot.
foundling: A deserted or exposed infant; a child found without a parent or owner. Foundling hospital, a hospital for foundlings.
foziness: The state of being fozy; spiritlessness; dullness. [Scot.] [The Whigs'] foziness can no longer be concealed. Blackwood's.
foliole: One of the distinct parts of a compound leaf; a leaflet.
forestage: (a) A duty or tribute payable to the king's foresters. (b) A service paid by foresters to the king.
foxglove: Any plant of the genus Digitalis. The common English foxglove (Digitalis purpurea) is a handsome perennial or biennial plant, whose leaves are used as a powerful medicine, both as a sedative and diuretic. See Digitalis. Pan through the pastures oftentimes hath run To pluck the speckled foxgloves from their stem. W. Browne.
footboard: 1. A board or narrow platfrom upon which one may stand or brace his feet; as: (a) The platform for the engineer and fireman of a locomotive. (b) The foot-rest of a coachman's box. 2. A board forming the foot of a bedstead. 3. A treadle.
fordable: Capable of being forded. -- Ford"a*ble*ness, n.
fourfooted: Having four feet; quadruped; as, fourfooted beasts.
foretime: The past; the time before the present. "A very dim foretime." J. C. Shairp.
founding: The art of smelting and casting metals.
forebeam: The breast beam of a loom.
foreside: 1. The front side; the front; esp., a stretch of country fronting the sea. 2. The outside or external covering. Spenser.
forbiddenly: In a forbidden or unlawful manner. Shak.
footstalk: 1. (Bot.) The stalk of a leaf or of flower; a petiole, pedicel, or reduncle. 2. (Zoöl.) (a) The peduncle or stem by which various marine animals are attached, as certain brachiopods and goose barnacles. (b) The stem which supports which supports the eye in decapod Crustacea; eyestalk. 3. (Mach.) The lower part of a millstone spindle. It rests in a step. Knight.
forciblefeeble: Seemingly vigorous, but really weak or insipid. He [Prof. Ayton] would purge his book of much offensive matter, if he struck out epithets which are in the bad taste of the forcible-feeble school. N. Brit. Review.
foreknowledge: Knowledge of a thing before it happens, or of whatever is to happen; prescience. If I foreknew, Foreknowledge had no influence on their fault. Milton.
forpine: To waste away completely by suffering or torment. (old) "Pale as a forpined ghost." Chaucer.
footnote: A note of reference or comment at the foot of a page.
formless: Shapeless; without a determinate form; wanting regularity of shape. -- Form"less*ly, adv. -- Form"less*ness, n.
forswear: 1. To reject or renounce upon oath; hence, to renounce earnestly, determinedly, or with protestations. I . . . do forswear her. Shak. 2. To deny upon oath. Like innocence, and as serenely bold As… | To swear falsely; to commit perjury. Shak.
forestick: Front stick of a hearth fire.
fortilage: A little fort; a blockhouse. (old) Spenser.
fourierist: One who adopts the views of Fourier.
fortune: 1. The arrival of something in a sudden or unexpected manner; chance; accident; luck; hap; also, the personified or deified power regarded as determining human success, apportioning happiness and… | 1. To make fortunate; to give either good or bad fortune to. (old) Chaucer. 2. To provide with a fortune. Richardson. 3. To presage; to tell the fortune of. (old) Dryden.
folder: One who, or that which, folds; esp., a flat, knifelike instrument used for folding paper.
foolscap: A writing paper made in sheets, ordinarily 16 x 13 inches, and folded so as to make a page 13 x 8 inches. See Paper.
folium: 1. A leaf, esp. a thin leaf or plate. 2. (Geom.) A curve of the third order, consisting of two infinite branches, which have a common asymptote. The curve has a double point, and a leaf-shaped loop; whence the name. Its equation is x3 + y3 = axy.
foliolate: Of or pertaining to leaflets; -- used in composition; as, bi- foliolate. Gray.
fordless: Without a ford. A deep and fordless river. Mallock.
forelay: 1. To lay down beforehand. These grounds being forelaid and understood. Mede. 2. To waylay. See Forlay. (old)
formalin: An aqueous solution of formaldehyde, used as a preservative in museums and as a disinfectant.
focimeter: (Photog.) An assisting instrument for focusing an object in or before a camera. Knight.
fossick: 1. (Mining) To search for gold by picking at stone or earth or among roots in isolated spots, picking over abandoned workings, etc.; hence, to steal gold or auriferous matter from another's claim. [Australia] 2. To search about; to rummage. A man who has fossicked in nature's byways. D. Macdonald.
foppery: 1. The behavior, dress, or other indication of a fop; coxcombry; affectation of show; showy folly. 2. Folly; foolery. Let not the sound of shallow foppery enter My sober house. Shak.
footmanship: Art or skill of a footman.
fogger: One who fogs; a pettifogger. (old) A beggarly fogger. Terence in English(1614)
forblack: Very black. (old) As any raven's feathers it shone forblack. Chaucer.
foveola: A small depression or pit; a fovea.
foxtail: 1. The tail or brush of a fox. 2. (Bot.) The name of several kinds of grass having a soft dense head of flowers, mostly the species of Alopecurus and Setaria. 3. (Metal.) The last cinders obtained in the fining process. Raymond. Foxtail saw, a dovetail saw. -- Foxtail wedging. See Fox wedge, under Fox.
foster: 1. To feed; to nourish; to support; to bring up. Some say that ravens foster forlorn children. Shak. 2. To cherish; to promote the growth of; to encourage; to sustain and promote; | To be nourished or trained up together. (old) Spenser.
forslow: To delay; to hinder; to neglect; to put off. (old) Bacon.
formative: 1. Giving form; having the power of giving form; plastic; as, the formative arts. The meanest plant can not be raised without seed, by any formative residing in the soil. Bentley. 2. | (a) That which serves merely to give form, and is no part of the radical, as the prefix or the termination of a word. (b) A word formed in accordance with some rule or usage, as from a root.
foment: 1. To apply a warm lotion to; to bathe with a cloth or sponge wet with warm water or medicated liquid. 2. To cherish with heat; to foster. (old) Which these soft fires . . . foment and warm. Milton. 3. To nurse to life or activity; to cherish and promote by excitements; to encourage; to abet; to instigate; -- used often in a bad sense; as, to foment ill humors. Locke.
forwander: To wander away; to go astray; to wander far and to weariness. (old)
formed: 1. (Astron.) Arranged, as stars in a constellation; as, formed stars. 2. (Biol.) Having structure; capable of growth and development; organized; as, the formed or organized ferments. See Ferment, n.
forth: 1. Forward; onward in time, place, or order; in advance from a given point; on to end; as, from that day forth; one, two, three, and so forth. Lucas was Paul's companion, at the leastway from the… | Forth from; out of. (old) Some forth their cabins peep. Donne.
forwarder: 1. One who forwards or promotes; a promoter. Udall. 2. One who sends forward anything; (Com.) one who transmits goods; a forwarding merchant. 3. (Bookbinding) One employed in forwarding.
foredate: To date before the true time; to antendate.
fowlerite: A variety of rhodonite, from Franklin Furnace, New Jersey, containing some zinc. FOWLER'S SOLUTION Fow"ler's so*lu"tion . An Fowler, an English physician who first brought it into use.
fordry: Entirely dry; withered. (old) "A tree fordry." Chaucer.
fornix: (a) An arch or fold; as, the fornix, or vault, of the cranium; the fornix, or reflection, of the conjuctiva. (b) Esp., two longitudinal bands of white nervous tissue beneath the lateral ventricles of the brain.
folkething: The lower house of the Danish Rigsdag, or Parliament. See Legislature, below.
fortunate: 1. Coming by good luck or favorable chance; bringing some good thing not foreseen as certain; presaging happiness; auspicious; as, a fortunate event; a fortunate concurrence of circumstances; a fortunate investment. 2. Receiving same unforeseen or unexpected good, or some good which was not dependent on one's own skill or efforts; favored with good forune; lucky. Syn.
forehand: 1. All that part of a horse which is before the rider. Johnson. 2. The chief or most important part. Shak. 3. Superiority; advantage; start; precedence. And, but for ceremony, such a wretch . . . | Done beforehand; anticipative. And so extenuate the forehand sin. Shak.
fornicatress: A woman guilty of fornication. Shak.
forceful: Full of or processing force; exerting force; mighty. -- Force"ful*ly, adv. Against the steed he threw His forceful spear. Dryden.
foreshortening: Representation in a foreshortened mode or way.
fossilist: One who is versed in the science of fossils; a paleontologist. Joseph Black.
forcemeat: Meat chopped fine and highly seasoned, either served up alone, or used as a stuffing. [Written also forced meat.]
forestaff: An instrument formerly used at sea for taking the altitudes of heavenly bodies, now superseded by the sextant; -- called also cross- staff. Brande & C.
foiler: One who foils or frustrates. Johnson.
forming: The act or process of giving form or shape to anything; as, in shipbuilding, the exact shaping of partially shaped timbers.
forel: A kind of parchment for book covers. See Forrill.
forefend: To hinder; to fend off; to avert; to prevent the approach of; to forbid or prohibit. See Forfend. God forefend it should ever be recorded in our history. Landor. It would be a far better work . . . to forefend the cruelty. I. Taylor.
foutra: A fig; -- a word of contempt. (old) A foutra for the world and wordlings base! Shak.
forgetfulness: 1. The quality of being forgetful; prononess to let slip from the mind. 2. Loss of remembrance or recollection; a ceasing to remember; oblivion. A sweet forgetfulness of human care. Pope. 3. Failure to bear in mind; careless omission; inattention; as, forgetfulness of duty. Syn. -- Forgetfulnes, Oblivion. Forgetfulness is Anglo-Saxon, and oblivion is Latin.
footbridge: A narrow bridge for foot passengers only.
footboy: A page; an attendant in livery; a lackey. Shak.
foolahs: , Foo"lahs` (, n. pl.; sing. Fulah, Foolan (. (Ethnol.) A peculiar African race of uncertain origin, but distinct from the negro tribes, inhabiting an extensive region of Western Soudan. Their color is brown or yellowish bronze. They are Mohammedans. Called also Fellatahs, Foulahs, and Fellani. Fulah is also used adjectively; as, Fulah empire, tribes, language.
forest: 1. An extensive wood; a large tract of land covered with trees; in the United States, a wood of native growth, or a tract of woodland which has never been cultivated. 2. (Eng. | Of or pertaining to a forest; sylvan. Forest fly. (Zoöl.) (a) One of numerous species of blood-sucking flies, of the family Tabanidæ, which attack both men and beasts. See Horse fly.
forsooth: In truth; in fact; certainly; very well; -- formerly used as an expression of deference or respect, especially to woman; now used ironically or contemptuously. A fit man, forsooth, to govern a realm!… | To address respectfully with the term forsooth. (old) The captain of the "Charles" had forsoothed her, though he knew her well enough and she him. Pepys.
foamy: Covered with foam; frothy; spumy. Behold how high the foamy billows ride! Dryden.
footpad: A highwayman or robber on foot.
forgiving: Disposed to forgive; inclined to overlook offenses; mild; merciful; compassionate; placable; as, a forgiving temper. -- For*giv"ing*ly, adv. -- For*giv"ing*ness, n. J. C. Shairp.
formyl: (a) A univalent radical, H.C:O, regarded as the essential residue of formic acid and aldehyde. (b) Formerly, the radical methyl, CH3.
formularization: The act of formularizing; a formularized or formulated statement or exhibition. C. Kingsley.
footlicker: A sycophant; a fawner; a toady. Cf. Bootlick. Shak.
forgo: To pass by; to leave. See 1st Forego. For sith [since] I shall forgoon my liberty At your request. Chaucer. And four [days] since Florimell the court forwent. Spenser. Note: This word in spelling has been confused with, and almost superseded by, forego to go before. Etymologically the form forgo is correct.
foliature: 1. Foliage; leafage. (old) Shuckford. 2. The state of being beaten into foil. Johnson.
foreknowingly: With foreknowledge. He who . . . foreknowingly loses his life. Jer. Taylor.
foulspoken: Using profane, scurrilous, slanderous, or obscene language. Shak.
foeman: An enemy in war. And the stern joy which warriors feel In foemen worthy of their steel. Sir W. Scott
foredeck: The fore part of a deck, or of a ship.
foolishness: 1. The quality of being foolish. 2. A foolish practice; an absurdity. The preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness. 1 Cor. i. 18.
footpace: 1. A walking pace or step. 2. A dais, or elevated platform; the highest step of the altar; a landing in a staircase. Shipley.
forsake: 1. To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart or withdraw from; to leave; as, false friends and flatterers forsake us in adversity. If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments. Ps. lxxxix. 30. 2. To renounce; to reject; to refuse. If you forsake the offer of their love. Shak. Syn. -- To abandon; quit; desert; fail; relinquish; give up;
forego: 1. To quit; to relinquish; to leave. Stay at the third cup, or forego the place. Herbert. 2. To relinquish the enjoyment or advantage of; to give up; to resign; to renounce; | To go before; to precede; -- used especially in the present and past participles. Pleasing remembrance of a thought foregone. Wordsworth. For which the very mother's face forewent The mother's…
forcement: The act of forcing; compulsion. (old) It was imposed upon us by constraint; And will you count such forcement treachery J. Webster.
follicle: 1. (Bot.) A simple podlike pericarp which contains several seeds and opens along the inner or ventral suture, as in the peony, larkspur and milkweed. 2. (Anat.) (a) A small cavity, tubular depression, or sac; as, a hair follicle. (b) A simple gland or glandular cavity; a crypt. (c) A small mass of adenoid tissue; as, a lymphatic follicle.
fountainless: Having no fountain; destitute of springs or sources of water. Barren desert, fountainless and dry. Milton.
fostress: A woman who feeds and cherishes; a nurse. B. Jonson.
foliated: 1. Having leaves, or leaflike projections; as, a foliated shell. 2. (Arch.) Containing, or consisting of, foils; as, a foliated arch. 3. (Min.) Characterized by being separable into thin plates or folia; as, graphite has a foliated structure. 4. (Geol.) Laminated, but restricted to the variety of laminated structure found in crystalline schist, as mica schist, etc.; schistose.
forwot: pres. indic. 1st & 3d pers. sing. of Forwete. (old) Chaucer.
foreremembered: Called to mind previously. Bp. Montagu.
foredeem: To recognize or judge in advance; to forebode. (old) Udall. Laugh at your misery, as foredeeming you An idle meteor. J. Webster. | To know or discover beforehand; to foretell. (old) Which [maid] could guess and foredeem of things past, present, and to come. Genevan Test.
formalist: One overattentive to forms, or too much confined to them; esp., one who rests in external religious forms, or observes strictly the outward forms of worship, without possessing the life and spirit of religion. As far a formalist from wisdom sits, In judging eyes, as libertines from wits. Young.
forelock: 1. The lock of hair that grows from the forepart of the head. 2. (Mech.) A cotter or split pin, as in a slot in a bolt, to prevent retraction; a linchpin; a pin fastening the cap-square of a gun. Forelock bolt, a bolt retained by a key, gib, or cotter passing through a slot.
fourdrinier: A machine used in making paper; -- so named from an early inventor of improvements in this class of machinery.
forfeiture: 1. The act of forfeiting; the loss of some right, privilege, estate, honor, office, or effects, by an offense, crime, breach of condition, or other act. Under pain of foreiture of the said goods. Hakluyt. 2. That which is forfeited; a penalty; a fine or mulct. What should I gain By the exaction of the forfeiture Shak. Syn. -- Fine; mulct; amercement; penalty.
forestall: 1. To take beforehand, or in advance; to anticipate. What need a man forestall his date of grief, And run to meet what he would most avoid Milton. 2. To take possession of, in advance of some one or something else, to the exclusion or detriment of the latter; to get ahead of; to preoccupy;
foraminiferous: 1. Having small openings, or foramina. 2. Pertaining to, or composed of, Foraminifera; as, foraminiferous mud.
forbearance: The act of forbearing or waiting; the exercise of patience. He soon shall findForbearance no acquittance ere day end. Milton. 2. The quality of being forbearing; indulgence toward offenders or enemies; long-suffering. Have a continent forbearance, till the speed of his rage goeShak. Syn. -- Abstinence; refraining; lenity; mildness.
forcite: A gelatin dynamite in which the dope is composed largely of sodium nitrate.
fossulate: Having, or surrounded by, long, narrow depressions or furrows.
fourteen: Four and ten more; twice seven. | 1. The sum of ten and four; forteen units or objects. 2. A symbol representing fourteen, as 14 or xiv.
fodientia: A group of African edentates including the aard-vark.
forefront: Foremost part or place. Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle. 2 Sam. xi. 15. Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, standing in the forefront for all time, the masters of those who know. J. C. Shairp.

foyer: 1. A lobby in a theater; a greenroom. 2. The crucible or basin in a furnace which receives the molten metal. Knight.
formalize: 1. To give form, or a certain form, to; to model. 2. To render formal. | To affect formality. (old) ales.
foralite: A tubelike marking, occuring in sandstone and other strata.

forehead: 1. The front of that part of the head which incloses the brain; that part of the face above the eyes; the brow. 2. The aspect or countenance; assurance. foredispose: To bestow beforehand. King James had by promise foredisposed the place on the Bishop of Meath. Fuller.
forestaller: One who forestalls; esp., one who forestalls the market. Locke.
forevouched: Formerly vouched or avowed; affirmed in advance. Shak.
fourierite: One who adopts the views of Fourier.
fourierism: The coöperative socialistic system of Charles Fourier, a Frenchman, who recommended the reorganization of society into small communities, living in common.
foredoom: To doom beforehand; to predestinate. Thou art foredomed to view the Stygian state. Dryden. | Doom or sentence decreed in advance. "A dread foredoom ringing in the ears of the guilty adult." Southey.
forecited: Cited or quoted before or above. Arbuthnot.
foreyard: The lowermost yard on the foremast. Note: [See Illust. of Ship.]
forerun: 1. To turn before; to precede; to be in advance of (something following). 2. To come before as an earnest of something to follow; to introduce as a harbinger; to announce. These signs forerun the death or fall of kings. Shak.
forslouthe: To lose by sloth or negligence. (old) Chaucer.
force: To stuff; to lard; to farce. Wit larded with malice, and malice forced with wit. Shak. | A waterfall; a cascade. [Prov. Eng.] To see the falls for force of the river Kent. T. Gray.
forworn: Much worn. (old) A silly man, in simple weeds forworn. Spenser.
forspeak: 1. To forbid; to prohibit. Shak. 2. To bewitch. (old) Drayton.
forficate: Deeply forked, as the tail of certain birds.
forebrace: A rope applied to the fore yardarm, to change the position of the foresail.
forester: 1. One who has charge of the growing timber on an estate; an officer appointed to watch a forest and preserve the game. 2. An inhabitant of a forest. Wordsworth. 3. A forest tree. foreign: 1. Outside; extraneous; separated; alien; as, a foreign country; a foreign government. "Foreign worlds." Milton. 2. forespurrer: One who rides before; a harbinger. (old) Shak.
fornicate: 1. Vaulted like an oven or furnace; arched. 2. (Bot.) Arching over; overarched. Gray. | To commit fornication; to have unlawful sexual intercourse.
fortalice: A small outwork of a fortification; a fortilage; -- called also fortelace.
fourfold: Four times; quadruple; as, a fourfold division. He snall restore the lamb fourfold. 2 Sam. xii. 6. | Four times as many or as much.
forkiness: The quality or state or dividing in a forklike manner.
foretaste: A taste beforehand; enjoyment in advance; anticipation. | 1. To taste before full possession; to have previous enjoyment or experience of; to anticipate. 2. To taste before another. "Foretasted fruit." Milton.
foredetermine: To determine or decree beforehand. Bp. Hopkins.
forlore: oForlese. (old) The beasts their caves, the birds their neforlore. Fairfax.
forum: 1. A market place or public place in Rome, where causes were judicially tried, and orations delivered to the people. 2. A tribunal; a court; an assembly empowered to hear and decide causes. He [Lord Camden] was . . . more eminent in the senate than in the forum. Brougham.
fosse: 1. (Fort.) A ditch or moat. 2. (Anat.) See Fossa. Fosse road. See Fosseway.
foreappoint: To set, order, or appoint, beforehand. Sherwood.
footcloth: Formerly, a housing or caparison for a horse. Sir W. Scott.
foraminous: Having foramina; full of holes; porous. Bacon.
formicid: Pertaining to the ants. -- n. One of the family Formicidæ, or ants.
forwrap: To wrap up; to conceal. (old) All mote be said and nought excused, nor hid, nor forwrapped. Chaucer.
forswat: Spent with heat; covered with sweat. (old) P. Sidney.
forever: 1. Through eternity; through endless ages, eternally. 2. At all times; always. fontal: Pertaining to a font, fountain, source, or origin; original; primitive. From the fontal light of ideas only can a man draw intellectual power. Coleridge.

foiling: The track of game (as deer) in the grass.
follicular: 1. Like, pertaining to, or consisting of, a follicles or follicles. 2. (Med.) Affecting the follicles; as, follicular pharyngitis.
fortread: To tread down; to trample upon. (old) In hell shall they be all fortroden of devils. Chaucer.

foreknow: To have previous knowledge of; to know beforehand. Who would the miseries of man foreknow Dryden.
fordo: 1. To destroy; to undo; to ruin. (old) This is the night That either makes me or fordoes me quite. Shak. 2. To overcome with fatigue; to exhaust. M. Arnold. All with weary task fordone. Shak.
foothalt: A disease affecting the feet of sheep.
foundation: 1. The act of founding, fixing, establishing, or beginning to erect. 2. That upon which anything is founded; that on which anything stands, and by which it is supported; the lowest and supporting layer of a superstructure; groundwork; basis. Behold, I lay in Zion, for a foundation, a stone . . . a precious corner stone, a sure foundation. Is. xxviii. 16.
folious: 1. Like a leaf; thin; unsubstantial. Sir T. Browne. 2. (Bot.) Foliose.
forecast: 1. To plan beforehand; to scheme; to project. He shall forecast his devices against the strongholds. Dan. xi. 24. 2. To foresee; to calculate beforehand, so as to provide for. | To contrive or plan beforehand. If it happen as I did forecast. Milton.
fox: 1. (Zoöl.) A carnivorous animal of the genus Vulpes, family Canidæ, of many species. The European fox (V. vulgaris or V. vulpes), the American red fox (V. fulvus), the American gray fox (V. | 1. forweary: To weary extremely; to dispirit. (old) Spenser.
foreigner: A person belonging to or owning allegiance to a foreign country; one not native in the country or jurisdiction under consideration, or not naturalized there; an alien; a stranger. formal: 1. Belonging to the form, shape, frame, external appearance, or organization of a thing. 2. forgivable: Capable of being forgiven; pardonable; venial. Sherwood.
fossilized: Converted into a fossil; antiquated; firmly fixed in views or opinions. A fossilized sample of confused provincialism. Earle.
forefather: One who precedes another in the line of genealogy in any degree, but usually in a remote degree; an ancestor. Respecting your forefathers, you would have been taught to respect yourselves. Burke. focus: 1. (Opt.) A point in which the rays of light meet, after being reflected or refrcted, and at which the image is formed; as, the focus of a lens or mirror. 2. (Geom.) A point so related to a conic… | To bring to a focus; to focalize; as, to focus a camera. R. Hunt.
